title: Systemic Pathogens: Structure, Tropism, and Spread
subject: Immunology and Microbiology (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers pathogens that spread from a mucosal entry point to cause systemic disease: parvovirus B19, Haemophilus influenzae type b, influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, the herpesviruses of mononucleosis and roseola, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Toxoplasma gondii. For each organism the chapter links structure, receptor, route of spread, and virulence factors to the disease they produce. Board questions rarely ask for a bare fact; they describe a patient or a laboratory finding and expect you to name the receptor, the genome type, or the toxin that explains it. If you can say why each organism reaches the tissue it damages and how that damage happens, you can reason through most of these questions.
prerequisites: Viral classification by genome (DNA or RNA, single or double stranded, positive or negative sense) and envelope
Gram stain, cell wall structure, and basic bacterial identification tests
Antigen presentation on MHC class I and II and T cell receptor recognition
Erythropoiesis, red cell life span, and the reticulocyte count

connections.how: Parvovirus B19 halts erythropoiesis, so its effect depends on red cell survival, linking it to hemolytic anemias and fetal hydrops.
M protein mimicry explains acute rheumatic fever, and streptococcal superantigens show how polyclonal T cell activation causes shock.
Rubella, parvovirus B19, and Toxoplasma cross the placenta, and the timing of infection predicts which developing tissues are damaged.
Loss of T cell control lets latent EBV drive lymphoproliferation and lets Toxoplasma cysts reactivate in the brain.
Influenza and measles damage airway defenses that set up bacterial pneumonia, and Hib, mumps, and measles reach the meninges and brain.

terms.def: The restriction of a pathogen to particular cells or tissues, set mainly by receptor distribution and the cell's ability to support replication.
A viral RNA genome complementary to mRNA, which must be transcribed by a polymerase carried in the virion before proteins can be made.
A viral RNA genome with the same sense as mRNA, which ribosomes can translate directly on entry.
A multinucleated cell formed when viral fusion proteins on an infected cell fuse it with neighboring cells.
Gradual change in influenza surface antigens from point mutations, producing strains that partly escape existing immunity.
Abrupt replacement of an influenza A hemagglutinin or neuraminidase subtype by reassortment of genome segments between strains.
A persistent infection in which the viral genome remains in the cell with few or no viral proteins made and no new virions released.
An IgM antibody produced during EBV infection that agglutinates sheep or horse red cells although it was not raised against them.
A microbial protein that binds MHC class II and the T cell receptor beta chain outside the peptide groove, activating a large fraction of all T cells.
Cross-reaction of antibodies or T cells raised against a microbial antigen with a structurally similar host antigen.
The host in which a parasite completes its sexual reproduction; for Toxoplasma gondii, members of the cat family.
The rapidly dividing invasive stage of Toxoplasma during acute infection and the slowly dividing stage that persists inside tissue cysts.

sections.title: Parvovirus B19: erythroid tropism and arrest of red cell production

blocks.text: Parvovirus B19 is one of the smallest DNA viruses that infect humans: a nonenveloped icosahedral capsid about 22 to 24 nm across that holds a linear single-stranded DNA genome of about 5.6 kb. The genome encodes no DNA polymerase, so the virus can replicate only in cells that are in S phase and supply the host replication machinery. Because it has no envelope, it resists drying and the solvent and detergent treatment that inactivates enveloped viruses in plasma products.

The receptor is P antigen (globoside), a glycosphingolipid on erythroid progenitors from the burst-forming and colony-forming units through the pronormoblast. Entry also needs coreceptors (alpha5beta1 integrin and Ku80), and productive infection needs a dividing cell, so these requirements together confine replication mainly to erythroid precursors. People who lack P antigen (the rare p blood group phenotype) are naturally resistant. P antigen is also present on placental trophoblast, endothelium, and fetal myocardium, which helps explain transplacental infection and fetal myocarditis.

Inside an infected precursor, the nonstructural protein NS1 is cytotoxic and triggers apoptosis, so the cells that should mature into red cells die. The marrow shows absent late erythroid forms and occasional giant pronormoblasts with glassy intranuclear inclusions. Viremia peaks about 1 week after exposure, and reticulocytes fall to near zero for about 7 to 10 days until neutralizing IgM and then IgG clear the virus. In a person who cannot make neutralizing antibody (advanced HIV, transplant immunosuppression, congenital immunodeficiency), viremia persists and causes chronic pure red cell aplasia.

B19 spreads by respiratory droplets, by blood products, and across the placenta. A person is most infectious during viremia, before any rash. The slapped-cheek rash of erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) in children and the symmetric small-joint arthropathy of adults, especially women, are immune complex effects that appear with antibody, when the person is no longer infectious. The fetus has a rapidly expanding red cell mass and red cells with a shorter life span, so arrest of erythropoiesis causes severe anemia, high-output heart failure, and nonimmune hydrops fetalis; the risk is greatest when maternal infection occurs in the first half of pregnancy.

blocks.title: Parvovirus B19 and transient aplastic crisis
steps: Respiratory droplets carry B19 to the bloodstream
Virus binds P antigen on dividing erythroid progenitors
NS1 triggers apoptosis of infected progenitors
Reticulocytes fall to near zero for about 7 to 10 days
Short red cell survival turns the pause into severe anemia
Neutralizing antibody clears virus; reticulocytes rebound
blocks.caption: The same marrow pause is trivial with normal red cell survival and dangerous when survival is short.

blocks.title: Why the same infection is mild in one child and severe in another
blocks.text: Normal red cells live about 120 days, so about 0.8 percent are removed each day. A 7-day production pause lowers hemoglobin by only about 5 to 6 percent, for example from 13 to about 12.3 g/dL, which goes unnoticed. In sickle cell disease red cells survive only about 10 to 20 days, so 5 to 10 percent are removed daily and the marrow normally compensates with a reticulocyte count often above 10 percent. Stop production for 7 days and roughly 40 percent of the red cell mass is lost: hemoglobin falls from a baseline of 8 to about 5 g/dL, and the reticulocyte count falls below 1 percent. A low reticulocyte count with falling hemoglobin points to an aplastic crisis, not a hemolytic crisis, in which reticulocytes would rise.

sections.title: Haemophilus influenzae type b: capsule, IgA protease, and growth factors

blocks.text: Haemophilus influenzae is a small, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus and facultative anaerobe whose only natural host is humans. Despite its name, it is a bacterium unrelated to the influenza virus. Strains are either encapsulated, with six capsular serotypes (a to f), or unencapsulated (nontypeable). Nontypeable strains cause mucosal infections such as otitis media, sinusitis, and bronchitis and rarely invade. Type b caused most invasive disease in young children before conjugate vaccination: meningitis, epiglottitis, bacteremia, pneumonia, septic arthritis, and cellulitis.

The type b capsule is polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP), a polymer of ribose, ribitol, and phosphate. This hydrophilic, negatively charged coat covers the surface structures that would otherwise activate the alternative complement pathway, so little C3b is deposited and phagocytes cannot bind the organism. Clearance from blood therefore depends on anti-PRP antibody, which fixes complement and opsonizes, and on the spleen, which removes poorly opsonized bacteria. PRP is a T cell independent antigen, and children under about 2 years respond poorly to polysaccharides. Maternal IgG protects for the first few months, which is why invasive Hib disease peaked between about 6 months and 2 years of age. Linking PRP to a protein carrier recruits T cell help and produces a protective, class-switched response in infants, the principle of the conjugate vaccine.

Other virulence factors help the organism colonize and inflame. IgA protease cleaves the hinge region of IgA1, separating the antigen-binding Fab fragments from Fc, so secretory antibody can no longer block adherence or agglutinate bacteria. Pili and other adhesins attach to nasopharyngeal epithelium, and lipooligosaccharide, a shorter form of endotoxin, drives inflammation in the meninges and airway. Spread is by respiratory droplets and contact with secretions; organisms colonize the nasopharynx, invade the bloodstream, and seed the meninges, epiglottis, joints, and lungs.

H influenzae cannot make heme or NAD+, so it needs both from its surroundings, as the table shows. Sheep blood agar contains both factors locked inside intact red cells and also contains NADases that destroy free NAD+. Heating blood agar to about 80 degrees C (176 degrees F) lyses the red cells, releases hemin and NAD+, and inactivates the NADases; the medium turns brown and is called chocolate agar.

blocks.title: Growth factors required by H influenzae
rows: Heme for cytochromes and catalase in aerobic respiration
Electron carrier for oxidation and reduction reactions
blocks.caption: Chocolate agar supplies both; unheated sheep blood agar supplies neither in usable form.

blocks.predict: On sheep blood agar, H influenzae grows only as tiny colonies close to a streak of Staphylococcus aureus. Why?
blocks.explain: S aureus lyses nearby red cells with its hemolysins, releasing hemin (X factor), and it secretes NAD+ (V factor). Only the area around the streak supplies both factors, so H influenzae grows there, a pattern called satellite growth.

sections.title: Influenza virus: hemagglutinin, neuraminidase, drift, and shift

blocks.text: Influenza viruses are orthomyxoviruses: enveloped viruses with helical nucleocapsids and a segmented, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome, with eight segments in influenza A and B. Because the genome is complementary to mRNA, the virion carries its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Unusually for an RNA virus, influenza transcribes and replicates in the nucleus, taking 5 prime caps from host pre-mRNA to prime its own transcripts. Types A, B, and C are defined by internal proteins; influenza A is further subtyped by its hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), as in H1N1 or H3N2.

Hemagglutinin is the attachment and fusion protein. It binds sialic acid on glycoproteins and glycolipids of respiratory epithelium; human strains prefer sialic acid in alpha2,6 linkage, abundant in the upper airway, whereas avian strains prefer alpha2,3 linkage. HA is made as HA0 and must be cleaved into HA1 and HA2 by trypsin-like proteases of the airway, which helps confine human infection to the respiratory tract. After endocytosis, the acid pH of the endosome changes HA shape and exposes the HA2 fusion peptide, which fuses the envelope with the endosomal membrane. The M2 proton channel acidifies the virion interior so the ribonucleoproteins separate and enter the nucleus.

Neuraminidase acts at the end of the cycle. New virions bud from the apical surface, and their HA would bind sialic acid on the cell and on each other; NA cleaves sialic acid so virions are released and do not clump. NA also cuts sialic acid in mucus, helping virus reach the epithelium. Blocking NA leaves new virions stuck to the cell surface, which shows its role. Antibody against HA neutralizes infection, while antibody against NA limits spread.

blocks.title: Influenza entry, replication, and release
steps: HA binds sialic acid on airway epithelium
Virus enters by endocytosis
Endosomal acid triggers HA fusion; M2 acidifies virion
Segments enter nucleus for transcription and replication
Virions bud from the apical membrane
NA cleaves sialic acid and releases virions
blocks.caption: HA works at entry and NA at exit; both are the main targets of protective antibody.

blocks.text: The virus kills ciliated columnar cells, so mucociliary clearance fails and the basement membrane is exposed; fever and myalgia come from cytokines such as interferons, IL-6, and TNF rather than from viremia. This damage sets up secondary bacterial pneumonia with S aureus, S pneumoniae, or H influenzae, often after initial improvement.

The viral polymerase lacks proofreading, so point mutations accumulate. Mutations in HA and NA antibody-binding sites are selected by population immunity, producing antigenic drift and yearly epidemics in influenza A and B. Antigenic shift requires two influenza A strains, often human and avian, to infect the same cell; segments are packaged in new combinations (reassortment), creating a virus with an HA or NA subtype few people have met. Only influenza A has animal reservoirs carrying many subtypes, so only A shifts. Pigs, whose airway carries both sialic acid linkages, can host both. The 1957 H2N2 and 1968 H3N2 pandemic viruses arose by reassortment of human and avian segments.

blocks.title: Antigenic drift versus antigenic shift
rows: Point mutations in HA and NA genes
blocks.caption: Drift is gradual and continuous; shift is abrupt and needs a segmented genome plus coinfection.

blocks.predict: Could measles virus undergo antigenic shift?
blocks.explain: No. Shift needs a segmented genome so whole genes can be swapped between strains. Measles has a single nonsegmented RNA, has no animal reservoir, and is antigenically stable with one serotype.
blocks.check: The drift and shift paragraph and the table.

blocks.text: Measles virus (genus Morbillivirus) and mumps virus (genus Orthorubulavirus, formerly Rubulavirus) are paramyxoviruses: enveloped viruses with a helical nucleocapsid and a single nonsegmented, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome that replicate in the cytoplasm. Each has an attachment protein (H in measles; HN, with hemagglutinin and neuraminidase activity, in mumps) and a fusion (F) protein. With no segments to reassort, each is antigenically stable with one serotype, so infection or vaccination gives lasting immunity.

F is made as F0 and cleaved by the host protease furin, exposing a hydrophobic fusion peptide. Unlike influenza HA, F works at neutral pH, so after the attachment protein binds, the envelope fuses directly with the plasma membrane. F on the surface of an infected cell fuses it with its neighbors, forming multinucleated syncytia that let virus spread cell to cell, out of reach of antibody. In measles, Warthin-Finkeldey cells are syncytial giant cells with many nuclei found in tonsils, lymph nodes, appendix, and Peyer patches during the prodrome.

Measles H binds SLAM (CD150) on activated lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and alveolar macrophages, which carry virus to lymph nodes and blood; it later binds nectin-4 on the basolateral surface of airway epithelium, from which virus is shed. Measles is airborne and among the most contagious human infections. The rash is produced by T cells attacking infected endothelium. Infection and loss of memory lymphocytes suppress immunity for months or longer, so pneumonia (the main cause of measles death) and otitis follow. Rarer outcomes are acute encephalitis and, years later, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis from persistent defective virus.

Mumps HN binds sialic acid. The virus replicates in upper airway epithelium and regional nodes, and viremia seeds glands and the nervous system. Inflammation inside tight capsules, such as the parotid fascia and the tunica albuginea of the testis, causes pain and, in the testis, pressure atrophy.

Rubella virus (genus Rubivirus) was classed as a togavirus and is now placed in its own family, Matonaviridae. It is enveloped with an icosahedral capsid and positive-sense single-stranded RNA that ribosomes translate directly, so no polymerase is packaged. Postnatal rubella is mild. Transplacental infection, most damaging in the first 12 weeks, inhibits cell division and injures vascular endothelium in developing organs, causing congenital rubella syndrome: cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis, with blueberry muffin skin lesions from dermal extramedullary hematopoiesis.

blocks.title: Measles, mumps, and rubella compared
rows: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; Koplik spots; rash from hairline down
Parotitis, orchitis after puberty, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis
Mild rash spreading from face, fading in about 3 days; postauricular and suboccipital nodes; arthralgia in women
blocks.caption: Measles and mumps share structure and F-mediated fusion; rubella differs in genome sense and family.

sections.title: EBV, HHV-6, and HHV-7: latency, lymphocyte tropism, and salivary spread

blocks.text: Herpesviruses are large enveloped viruses with an icosahedral capsid, a protein tegument, and linear double-stranded DNA; they replicate and assemble in the nucleus. After primary infection the genome circularizes into an episome and expresses few or no viral proteins, so infected cells are nearly invisible to CD8 T cells. This latency lasts for life, and the virus reactivates when T cell immunity weakens. Healthy carriers shed EBV, HHV-6, and HHV-7 intermittently in saliva, so most people acquire them in childhood from family members, and EBV acquired in adolescence spreads by kissing.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, HHV-4, a gammaherpesvirus) replicates in oropharyngeal epithelium and tonsillar B cells. Its envelope glycoprotein gp350 binds CD21 (complement receptor 2, the receptor for the C3d fragment), and gp42 binds MHC class II as a coreceptor to trigger fusion; mature B cells carry both. Latent proteins drive the infected B cell: EBNA-1 keeps the episome in dividing cells, LMP-1 mimics a constantly active CD40 and switches on NF-kappaB, and LMP-2A mimics B cell receptor signaling. Infected B cells proliferate and then persist in memory B cells for life.

The findings of infectious mononucleosis come mostly from the immune response. CD8 T cells expand massively against infected B cells and appear in blood as atypical lymphocytes (large cells with abundant cytoplasm indented by neighboring red cells); EBV infects the B cells, but the atypical cells are T cells. Lymphoid expansion produces exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly with a stretched capsule that can rupture, and mild hepatitis. Polyclonal B cell activation yields heterophile IgM that agglutinates sheep or horse red cells, the basis of the Monospot test; it is often negative early in illness and in children under about 4 years. When T cell control fails, EBV-driven B cells can become lymphoma, and EBV is linked to Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

HHV-6 and HHV-7 are betaherpesviruses (genus Roseolovirus) that infect CD4 T cells. HHV-7 uses CD4 itself as its receptor, HHV-6B uses CD134 (OX40), and HHV-6A uses CD46; HHV-6 latency is mainly in monocytes and macrophages, and HHV-7 latency in CD4 T cells. Nearly all children are infected by about 2 to 3 years of age. Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, sixth disease), caused mainly by HHV-6B, affects children about 6 months to 2 years old: 3 to 5 days of high fever, often 39 to 40 degrees C (102 to 104 degrees F), which can provoke febrile seizures, then a rosy, blanching maculopapular rash on the trunk as the fever falls and the immune response takes hold.

blocks.title: Herpesviruses of mononucleosis and roseola
rows: gp350 binds CD21; gp42 binds MHC class II; B cells and oropharyngeal epithelium
CD4 T cells; HHV-7 binds CD4, HHV-6B binds CD134
HHV-6: monocytes and macrophages; HHV-7: CD4 T cells
Infectious mononucleosis in adolescents and young adults
Roseola infantum in infants and toddlers
Atypical CD8 T cells; heterophile antibody
Heterophile negative; diagnosis is mostly clinical
blocks.caption: All are enveloped dsDNA viruses spread by saliva with lifelong latency; they differ in which lymphocyte they enter.

sections.title: Streptococcus pyogenes: identification, M protein, and superantigens

blocks.text: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus) is a gram-positive coccus that grows in chains and colonizes the pharynx and skin. It spreads by respiratory droplets and direct contact. Its laboratory identity rests on a sequence of tests that separates it from staphylococci and from other streptococci, summarized below. Complete (beta) hemolysis comes from streptolysin S, which is oxygen stable, and streptolysin O, which is oxygen labile and immunogenic; antibody to streptolysin O (ASO) is the classic marker of recent infection.

blocks.title: Identifying S pyogenes
rows: From alpha-hemolytic S pneumoniae and viridans streptococci
Supports group A; group B is negative
blocks.caption: Catalase first, then hemolysis, then bacitracin is the standard decision path.

blocks.text: M protein is a coiled-coil fibrillar protein anchored in the cell wall that projects from the surface. It binds factor H and C4b-binding protein, host regulators that inactivate C3b, and it binds fibrinogen, which coats the bacterium. Little opsonin remains on the surface, so neutrophils cannot ingest the organism unless antibody to that particular M protein is present. The N-terminal end is hypervariable, giving more than 200 M types, so immunity is type specific and repeated infections occur. A hyaluronic acid capsule, chemically identical to host hyaluronan and therefore nonimmunogenic, and C5a peptidase, which limits neutrophil recruitment, add to this defense.

The conserved regions of M protein share epitopes with cardiac myosin, tropomyosin, and other host proteins. Antibodies and T cells raised against pharyngeal infection cross-react with heart, joints, and brain, causing acute rheumatic fever about 2 to 4 weeks later, a type II hypersensitivity reaction; carditis with valvulitis, especially of the mitral valve, is the lasting damage. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a different mechanism, immune complex (type III) injury after pharyngeal or skin infection with nephritogenic strains.

Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins A and C are superantigens encoded by temperate bacteriophages, so only lysogenized strains make them. A conventional peptide antigen activates about 0.001 to 0.01 percent of T cells; a superantigen activates every T cell that uses a matching V beta region, up to about 20 percent. The cytokine surge produces fever and dilation of dermal capillaries. Scarlet fever follows pharyngitis, usually in school-age children: a diffuse, fine, sandpaper-like erythematous rash that starts on the neck and upper trunk, deepens in skin folds (Pastia lines), spares the area around the mouth (circumoral pallor), with a strawberry tongue and later peeling of the hands and feet. At its extreme the same mechanism causes streptococcal toxic shock syndrome with capillary leak and multiorgan failure.

blocks.title: How a streptococcal superantigen causes scarlet fever and shock
steps: Toxin binds MHC class II outside the peptide groove
Same toxin binds the TCR beta chain variable region
Up to about 20 percent of T cells activate
Massive IL-2, interferon-gamma, TNF, and IL-1 release
Fever, dermal vasodilation, and diffuse erythematous rash
Severe cases: capillary leak, hypotension, organ failure
blocks.caption: No antigen processing or peptide specificity is needed, which is why so many T cells respond at once.

sections.title: Toxoplasma gondii: life cycle and routes of human infection

blocks.text: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan of the phylum Apicomplexa, the group that includes Plasmodium. It has three infectious stages: the sporozoite inside an oocyst, the rapidly dividing tachyzoite of acute infection, and the slowly dividing bradyzoite inside a tissue cyst. Members of the cat family are the definitive hosts because only they support the sexual cycle. Almost any warm-blooded animal, including humans, livestock, and rodents, can be an intermediate host, carrying tissue cysts but never producing oocysts.

A cat is infected by eating prey with tissue cysts or by swallowing oocysts. Bradyzoites invade the cat's intestinal epithelium, multiply asexually, and then form male and female gametes; fertilization produces oocysts. After a first infection the cat sheds very large numbers of unsporulated oocysts in feces for about 1 to 2 weeks. Oocysts need 1 to 5 days in the environment to sporulate and become infectious, and then survive in moist soil and water for many months. Fresh feces are therefore not infectious, while soil, garden produce, and unchanged litter can be.

blocks.title: Toxoplasma gondii life cycle
steps: Sexual cycle in cat intestinal epithelium
Unsporulated oocysts shed in cat feces
Oocysts sporulate in soil in 1 to 5 days
Intermediate host ingests sporulated oocysts
Tachyzoites spread; bradyzoite cysts form in muscle and brain
Cat eats prey with tissue cysts
blocks.caption: Humans enter as intermediate hosts by swallowing sporulated oocysts or tissue cysts in undercooked meat; the cycle continues only through cats.

blocks.text: Humans are infected by swallowing sporulated oocysts in soil, water, unwashed produce, or litter; by eating tissue cysts in undercooked meat such as pork, lamb, or venison; across the placenta; and rarely through organ transplant or transfusion. Digestion releases sporozoites or bradyzoites, which invade the intestinal epithelium and become tachyzoites. Tachyzoites enter cells actively using secretory organelles of the apical complex and live in a parasitophorous vacuole that does not fuse with lysosomes. They divide until the cell bursts and spread through blood and lymph, often inside monocytes, to almost any nucleated cell.

Dendritic cell IL-12 drives NK cells and T cells to make interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages and pushes the parasite into the bradyzoite stage inside tissue cysts in brain, retina, and skeletal and cardiac muscle, where it persists for life. Primary infection in an immunocompetent person is usually silent or a mononucleosis-like illness with cervical lymphadenopathy and a negative heterophile test. If CD4 counts fall below about 100 cells per microliter, cysts rupture and tachyzoites cause encephalitis with multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions.

Congenital infection needs tachyzoites in maternal blood, so it follows primary infection during pregnancy, or reactivation in a severely immunosuppressed mother; an immunocompetent woman infected well before conception almost never transmits. As the placenta grows, the chance of transmission rises across pregnancy while fetal damage becomes less severe, so early infection causes the worst disease and late infection is often silent at birth, with chorioretinitis appearing later. The classic findings are chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications scattered through the brain, unlike the periventricular calcifications of congenital cytomegalovirus.

blocks.predict: A pregnant woman with long-standing antibody to Toxoplasma and normal immunity eats undercooked lamb. Is her fetus at risk of congenital toxoplasmosis?
blocks.explain: Very little. Her existing immunity controls new parasites before tachyzoites circulate in large numbers, and congenital disease requires tachyzoites in maternal blood, which is mainly a feature of primary infection during pregnancy.
blocks.check: The paragraph on congenital infection and the role of interferon-gamma.

integration.text: Each organism in this chapter is explained by where it enters, which receptor it uses, and how the host responds. Receptors set tropism: P antigen sends parvovirus B19 to erythroid precursors, CD21 sends EBV to B cells, CD4 and CD134 send HHV-6 and HHV-7 to helper T cells, and sialic acid linkage restricts influenza to the airway. Genome structure sets variability: only the segmented influenza A genome can shift, while nonsegmented measles and mumps remain single serotypes. Many of the clinical findings are immune effects rather than direct viral damage, including the rash of fifth disease, the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis, the measles rash, rheumatic fever, and superantigen shock.

Three organisms cross the placenta, and each injures the fetus in a way that follows from its biology: parvovirus stops red cell production and causes hydrops, rubella blocks cell division during organogenesis, and Toxoplasma tachyzoites destroy brain and retina. Immune status changes the picture. Asplenia and absent antibody leave encapsulated Hib unchecked, absent neutralizing antibody turns parvovirus into chronic red cell aplasia, and T cell failure lets latent EBV and Toxoplasma escape control. These are generalizations, and individual strains, host genetics, and the timing of exposure all modify the outcome.

summary: Parvovirus B19 is a nonenveloped ssDNA virus that binds P antigen and kills dividing erythroid progenitors, halting red cell production for about a week; this is serious only when red cell survival is short, as in hemolysis or the fetus.
Hib is a gram-negative coccobacillus whose PRP capsule blocks complement and phagocytosis; IgA protease aids colonization, and growth needs X (hemin) and V (NAD+) factors supplied by chocolate agar.
Influenza hemagglutinin binds sialic acid and fuses in the acid endosome; neuraminidase releases new virions.
Drift is point mutation in HA and NA causing epidemics; shift is reassortment of segments in influenza A causing pandemics.

Measles and mumps are nonsegmented negative-sense paramyxoviruses whose F protein fuses cells at neutral pH, forming syncytia such as Warthin-Finkeldey cells; rubella is a positive-sense virus that damages the first-trimester fetus.
EBV enters B cells through CD21 and persists in memory B cells; the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis are reactive CD8 T cells.
HHV-6 and HHV-7 infect CD4 T cells, spread by saliva, and cause roseola with high fever followed by rash.
S pyogenes is catalase negative, beta-hemolytic, and bacitracin sensitive; M protein blocks opsonization and mimics cardiac proteins.
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens that bind MHC class II and TCR V beta outside the groove, causing scarlet fever and toxic shock.
Toxoplasma reproduces sexually only in cats; humans ingest sporulated oocysts or tissue cysts, and tachyzoites cross the placenta after primary maternal infection.
